newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade turnaround seen best bet to help yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade turnaround seen best bet to help yen.

text.p: Japan briefly brandished the threat of intervention on Thursday to prop up the flagging yen, but analysts said it would likely take a turnaround in Tokyo's trade gap with Washington to halt the yen's slide.

Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for his influence on exchange rates, said Japanese monetary authorities would intervene in currency markets at a time when such a move would be effective.

"When we judge that there is really harm being done to the Japanese economy, we will conduct it (intervention) when the timing is effective," Sakakibara was quoted as telling a ruling Liberal Democratic Party panel on foreign affairs.
The dollar -- which has powered higher on a daily basis with few signs that a retreat is at hand -- dipped on the remarks, carried by Japan's Jiji news agency.
But it quickly came off its lows after dealers dismissed the comments as hot air.
On Wednesday the greenback touched a 47-month high of 122.75 yen.
"I think these remarks do not mean that there will be immediate intervention (by the Bank of Japan) when we read and think about them carefully," said a dealer at a trust bank.
The yen has declined steadily since touching a global high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995, but the pace of the fall has picked up of late on a plethora of fundamental factors.
Tokyo has reacted to the slide with a barrage of comments first taken as hinting at intervention to defend the currency but more recently seen as implying only jawboning was in store.
Last week Japanese public television reported that the central bank had intervened to buy yen but many traders were sceptical, saying they could detect no evidence of this.
The United States, meanwhile, has stuck to a strong-dollar stance despite some complaints from American exporters that they are being hurt.

Prospects that Japan will keep its interest rates at rock-bottom levels to bolster its economic recovery while the United States tightens credit mean monetary policy is unlikely to break the yen's fall any time soon, economists said.
And yen-buying intervention that flies in the face of fundamentals would be of limited impact at best, they added.

"Intervention might work if it's concerted enough and at the right time, but if you're trying to prop up the yen you are more likely to succeed if interest rates are rising at the same time," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers.
The best hope for boosting the yen thus rests with a rise in Tokyo's trade surplus with Washington, signs of which have already emerged.
"The trade account should become positive for the yen in due course," Jones said. "I think the rise will surprise everyone."
Japan's trade surplus with the United States fell 16.5 percent to 3.55 trillion yen ($29.0 billion) in 1996, but data for December released last week showed a 7.8 percent rise for the month.

A rising surplus could spark fresh trade friction that would in turn weaken the dollar against the yen. In the past, U.S. officials have seen a strong yen as a way of forcing Japan to open its markets to American goods.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Wednesday that Washington would keep close watch on trade data.

"I don't yet know what the trend will be, but it's something that we want to keep an eye on and we want to be sure if there is any uptick it is not because of either new, or the persistance of old, market barriers," she said. ($1=122 yen)
